opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the thing I like most is that it just removes a whole category of tedium that used to eat up a surprising amount of time. A lot of real-world information doesn't come in a nice clean spreadsheet. It's a PDF someone exported from some old system, or a table that got pasted into an email and lost all its structure, or a bunch of notes where every person used a slightly different format. Before, you'd either write some brittle little parsing script that broke the moment the format shifted, or you'd just sit there copying and pasting by hand.

With Claude, I can just drop the mess in and say, "Turn this into a CSV with these columns," or "Pull out every date and the decision that was made," and it handles the weirdness. It figures out that this row is actually a continuation of the one above it, or that "Q3" and "July–Sept" mean the same thing. That kind of fuzzy judgment is exactly what's hard to encode in regular code but pretty easy for a language model.

And I think there's something nice about it from a personal perspective, too. Working on Claude, it's a bit of a satisfying loop: you're building the thing, and then you use the thing to make your own work less annoying. You do still want to spot-check the output, especially if it matters, but even with that verification step it's often dramatically faster. It's one of those use cases where the value is really obvious the first time you try it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they can drop in messy PDFs, pasted tables, or inconsistent notes and ask Claude to convert or extract information, without first cleaning up or reformatting the data.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing I like most is that I just don't have to think about the format anymore. So much of my day used to be this low-level grunt work of: here's a table someone pasted into Slack where the columns don't line up, here's a CSV that's actually tab-separated, here's a screenshot of a spreadsheet, here's a log file where half the lines are JSON and half are stack traces. And before, every one of those was a little bespoke parsing problem. You'd write a regex, it'd break on row 400, you'd fix it, and twenty minutes later you've still barely looked at the actual data.

With Claude I can just paste the thing in and say, "turn this into a clean table," or "pull out every error and the timestamp it happened," and it mostly just works. It's remarkably tolerant of inconsistency: a column that's sometimes empty, a date that's written three different ways, a header that got repeated halfway down because someone concatenated two files. A human intern would figure that out from context, and the model does too. That's the part that still feels a little magical to me, because historically computers were extremely literal and if you got one delimiter wrong everything fell over.

The other thing I'd say is that it moves the conversation to the right level of abstraction. Instead of me spending my attention on "how do I get this into pandas," I'm spending it on "what does this data actually say, and what's the next question." You can go back and forth: "okay, now group that by user," "actually, drop the ones from before Tuesday." It's much closer to how you'd work with a colleague who happens to be very fast and very patient.

I do want to add the caveat, though, because I think about this stuff a lot: for anything that matters, I still check it. These models are good, but if there's a subtle ambiguity in the data, they'll sometimes resolve it confidently in a way you didn't intend. So I'll ask it to show me the intermediate steps, or spot-check a few rows against the original. The nice thing is that even with that checking, it's dramatically faster than doing it by hand. It turns a chore into something that's basically free, and I think that changes which questions you bother to ask in the first place.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they can paste awkwardly formatted data into Claude and ask it to make a clean table or extract errors, without first reformatting it.

astra-6.text: One thing I really like is that you don’t have to clean everything up before you give it to Claude. You can paste in a messy chunk of text or a table whose formatting got mangled, and ask it to pull out the information you care about. That’s useful because getting information into the right format can otherwise be most of the work. You still need to check that it’s interpreted things correctly, but it makes that first pass much easier.

r001.rationale: It says users can paste messy or mangled text and tables into Claude and ask it to extract information without cleaning or reformatting them first.

sol-6.1.text: One thing I particularly like is being able to give it information in whatever form I happen to have it. If I’ve got a messy table or a bunch of notes with inconsistent formatting, I can just paste them in and say what I want out. I don’t have to do all this tidying up before I can start asking useful questions. It makes a lot of small tasks worth doing that otherwise would feel like too much hassle.

r001.rationale: The response says messy tables or inconsistently formatted notes can be pasted into Claude and queried without tidying them first.
